title: How to Examine Your Day (the Daily Examen)
excerpt: Most of us end the day by collapsing, not by looking. The examen is the ancient practice of looking back over a single day with God before the dark takes it from you.
body:
We live our days and almost never look at them. We move from task to task, react to whatever comes, and fall into bed already half asleep, and the day closes over us unexamined. Then we wonder why we keep making the same mistakes, why the same sins return, why God feels distant when we have not stopped long enough all day to notice him. The unexamined day is the one that runs us instead of the one we live.

The examen is a simple, ancient remedy. It comes to us most clearly through Ignatius of Loyola in the sixteenth century, who taught it as a daily practice of reviewing the day in the presence of God. You do not need his whole spiritual system to use it. You need ten minutes and the willingness to look honestly at the day you just lived. It is one of the most quietly powerful disciplines I know.

## Begin by getting still and remembering you are not alone

Find a few minutes at the end of the day, before sleep takes you. Sit down. Take a few slow breaths. Before you review anything, simply remember that you are in the presence of God, who was with you through every hour you are about to examine, and who looks on you with love, not with a clipboard. This is not an interrogation. It is a conversation with the One who walked the whole day beside you.

## Look back with gratitude

The first movement is gratitude, and it is first for a reason. Before you examine anything for failure, walk back through the day and notice the gifts. The good cup of coffee. The unexpected kindness. The work that went well. The face of someone you love. Gratitude trains the eye to see grace where you would otherwise see only events.

This is not forced positivity. It is attention. Most days contain far more grace than we register in the moment, because we are too busy living them to notice. The examen slows you down enough to see what God was quietly handing you all day.

## Notice where God was

Next, walk through the day again and ask a different question. Where was God in this day, and where did I sense his presence or his absence? Notice the moments you felt drawn toward love, toward patience, toward courage, toward joy. Notice the moments you felt pulled the other way, toward fear, resentment, despair, self-protection. Ignatius called these consolation and desolation. You do not need the vocabulary. You need only the honesty to ask what was happening underneath the day.

This is where self-knowledge grows. Over weeks, patterns emerge. You begin to see what consistently pulls you toward God and what consistently pulls you away, and that knowledge is gold for the soul.

## Face your failures honestly

Then comes the harder part. Walk through the day and ask where you failed. Where were you unkind, impatient, dishonest, proud? Where did you choose the small selfish thing? Do not rush past this and do not wallow in it. Name the failure plainly, the way you would name a fact, and then bring it to God, who already saw it and already loves you.

This is confession folded into the day, and it keeps short accounts. Sin that is named the night it happened does not get to fester and grow roots. The examen catches it early, while it is still small enough to confess and release.

## Look ahead to tomorrow

Finally, turn toward the day to come. Is there a meeting you dread, a conversation you have been avoiding, a temptation you can already see coming? Bring it to God now, while it is still tomorrow and not yet a crisis. Ask for what you will need. Then release the day you just lived, hand it to God, and let yourself sleep.

## Keep it short and keep it daily

The examen works because it is daily, not because it is long. Ten minutes is plenty. The temptation will be to skip it on tired nights, which are exactly the nights it helps most. Attach it to something fixed, lying down in bed, the last few minutes before you sleep, so it does not depend on willpower you have already spent. A short examen done every day will reshape your self-knowledge more than a long one done occasionally.

## This week

Each night before sleep, take ten minutes and walk through five steps. Remember God is present. Give thanks for three specific gifts from the day. Notice one moment you felt close to God and one you felt far. Name one failure and bring it to him. Then ask for what you will need tomorrow. Do it all seven nights, even the nights you are too tired to want to.

The day will close over you either way. The only question is whether you look at it first.
